title.text: Archdiocesan Shrine of Santa Teresa de Avila

title_en.text: Archdiocesan Shrine of Santa Teresa de Avila

tagline.text: A coral-stone archdiocesan shrine in Talisay, built after the parish became independent in 1836

location.label: Location
location.text: V. H. Garces Street, Poblacion, Talisay City, Cebu

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–May dry season (Oct 15 feast period separate)

children.text: This coral-stone church in Poblacion, Talisay City, south of Cebu City, began to be built when the parish became independent in 1836. It was declared an archdiocesan shrine in 2007 and is busiest on the saint's feast day, October 15.
The Archdiocesan Shrine of Santa Teresa de Avila is a Roman Catholic church in Poblacion, the center of Talisay City, Cebu. It lies
about 12 km

south of central Cebu City, so it is an easy stop on a day around the city. Some travel sites list an address in the Mananga area, but the parish's own information and Wikipedia both point to V. H. Garces Street, Poblacion, Talisay City, so use that address when you navigate.

In Spanish colonial times Talisay belonged to the Augustinian friars and was at first a visita of the parish of San Nicolas. A royal decree was signed on April 25, 1836, and on August 16 of that year the town became an independent parish under Fr. Juan Soriano, taking Saint Teresa of Avila as its patron. Construction is said to have begun in 1836 and continued until about 1848. The building you see today was shaped by later typhoon damage, war damage, post-war restoration and expansion.

The church's history is worth a moment. A typhoon destroyed the clay-tile roof, and records say it was re-roofed with iron sheets in 1877, while one local blog says a new church was built in 1880 and finished in 1881. The two accounts do not fully match, so it is safest not to state exactly what work was done in that period. The interior was decorated in 1894, and near the end of World War II the church and the neighboring convent were badly damaged and the parish records were lost. Post-war restoration was led by Fr. Teofilo Camomot, who is said to have lowered the roof at that time. The patron, Teresa of Avila, was born in Avila, Spain, in 1515 and was a Carmelite nun who founded prayer-centered convents and wrote The Way of Perfection and The Interior Castle; she was canonized in 1622 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1970. According to local tradition, Fr. Soriano, a native of Avila, brought her image in 1836 and placed the new parish under her protection.

The architecture is described as Greco-Roman (Doric) and is built of coral stone. The facade has two bell towers joined by a balustraded portico, and the original plan was cruciform with two semicircular transepts. Inside are five gilded altars, with a large round chandelier hanging above the crossing. Wikipedia gives the size as 72 m long and 33 m wide, but the building includes added wings, so treat the figures as a rough guide. On the feast day, October 15, 2007, then Archbishop of Cebu Cardinal Ricardo Vidal declared the parish an archdiocesan shrine. He explained that a shrine needs an old church, a tradition of people praying there regularly, and a priest ready to care for pilgrims. Some shrine write-ups call it the only shrine in the Philippines dedicated to the saint, but the archdiocese has not confirmed this wording, so take it as a reference only. It is not a flashy tourist attraction. Instead, it lets you see both the daily faith of a southern Cebu city and colonial-era church architecture. If you time your visit around Mass, English and Cebuano Masses are held in turn.

blocks.title: Coral-stone facade and twin bell towers

children.text: The Greco-Roman facade has two bell towers joined by a balustraded portico. The building was badly damaged in World War II, but the facade is known to have survived largely intact. At sunset the coral stone turns warm in color, which makes for good photos.

blocks.title: Five gilded altars and a large chandelier

children.text: Inside are five gold-leafed altars, and a large round chandelier hangs above the crossing. The original stone walls and arched windows remain between the two added wings, so it is fun to tell the old parts from the new.

blocks.title: The vested statue of Saint Teresa

children.text: The main altar holds a statue of the saint dressed in an embroidered Carmelite habit. She holds a quill and a book, and the statue is described as one of the oldest vested (de vestir) images in Cebu.

blocks.title: Our Lady of Joy (Birhen sa Kalipay)

children.text: Alongside the saint's statue, the altar holds Nuestra Señora de la Consolación y Correa, whom locals call Birhen sa Kalipay. A celebration in her honor is said to take place on the eve of the feast.

blocks.title: A priest's tomb in a small chapel

children.text: One of the small chapels inside is said to hold the tomb of an early priest. Some accounts suggest he may have been Fr. Soriano's predecessor, but this is not confirmed. If you would like a guide, politely ask at the parish office outside Mass times.
The saint's feast day is
October 15

every year. According to news reports, a "Walk with St. Teresa" procession is held in early October, a river procession takes place during the novena, and a grand procession is held on the feast day itself. Check the parish Facebook page each year for the exact schedule.

blocks.title: What the archdiocesan shrine status means

children.text: When the shrine was declared in 2007, a plenary indulgence could be obtained on the 15th of each month for one year, and processions walking at least 1 km to the shrine were said to bring spiritual benefits at any time. That period has ended, so ask the parish about current rules. You do not need to be a believer to observe quietly.
Leave Cebu City and arrive at Poblacion, Talisay. Allow about
30–60 minutes
for the trip, depending on traffic.
Start with the facade and photograph the twin bell towers and the coral-stone walls.
Go into the nave and quietly look at the gilded altars, the chandelier and the statue of the saint. Please avoid taking photos during Mass.
Buy a candle at a shop near the church and say a short prayer, or stroll the nearby market street.

There are several Masses from morning to evening on Sundays, so if you only want to look around, the time between Masses is much quieter. Whether inner areas such as the chapel and the tomb are open varies from day to day, so ask at the office first.

items.title: Half day combined with Cebu City
items.subtitle: Talisay church and Cebu City pilgrim sites

children.text: Visit the Talisay church first and look around the nave and facade.
Head toward Cebu City.
Have lunch in downtown Cebu City.
Continue to the Basilica del Santo Niño and Magellan's Cross.
A direct flight from Manila (NAIA) to Mactan–Cebu International Airport (CEB) takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
From the airport, you head toward Cebu City and then continue south to Talisay. A Grab or taxi is the simplest way.
Flight times and fares vary by airline, so check before booking.
Poblacion, Talisay is
about 12 km
south of central Cebu City.
Jeepneys, buses and vans run toward the south, and you need to check the fare locally. Routes and numbers can change, so ask the driver or terminal staff whether the vehicle goes to Talisay.
If you get off in Poblacion, the church is within walking distance. A ride-hailing taxi (Grab) can take you right to the church.
Giving V. H. Garces Street as the destination helps the driver find it easily.

Cebu has a dry season from December to May, with less rain and comfortable walking weather. A church visit is mostly indoors, so rain matters little, but in the rainy season roads get congested and trips take longer.

Around the October 15 feast, the area becomes very crowded with processions and Masses, and traffic may be controlled. Come then if you want the atmosphere, and on a weekday morning if you want to look at the architecture quietly.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The most comfortable time for visiting the church and walking.
You sweat a lot at midday, so a morning visit is recommended.
The October 15 feast is held. Be ready for rain and crowds.

Talisay is a satellite city of Cebu City, so there are not many large hotels around the church. Most travelers stay in Cebu City or on Mactan Island and visit as a day trip. If the timing works, pairing it with other pilgrim sites in Cebu City makes an efficient one-day route.

Around Poblacion there are local eateries and market stalls where you can have a simple meal or a snack. If you are looking for lechon, the roast pig Cebu is known for, or local snacks, take a lap around the market street. Opening hours vary by business, so it is best to check before you go.

A church visit fits nicely into the middle of a Cebu City itinerary. You can see the church early in the morning and return to the city for lunch, or drop by in the afternoon to match the evening Mass. Either way, avoid the rush-hour periods, when traffic is heavy and travel takes longer.
A church is a place of faith. Wear modest clothing that covers your shoulders and knees.
Avoid photos and conversation during Mass, and enter and leave quietly.
Masses are held many times on Sundays, from early morning to evening, so if you only want to look around, the time between Masses is best.
Weekday Masses are held in the morning and evening, so plan your schedule around them. Times can change, so check the latest announcements.
The parish office phone is (032) 272-8091, and announcements are also posted on Facebook under ASPSTA.
Traffic is controlled around the feast day, so decide where you will get off before you take a Grab.
Carry small cash for candles, offerings and snacks.
The coral stone looks its best in photos in the early morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low. Check permits and local rules before flying a drone.
During Mass and events, worship comes before sightseeing, so check the schedule before you visit.
Mass times, prayer times and procession schedules can change, so check the parish announcements before you visit.
During the feast and other big events, keep your belongings and valuables in front of your body.
If you do not follow the dress code, you may be asked to change.
Check jeepney and bus routes and fares locally, and ask about the destination before boarding.
Do not touch the statues or altars, and do not climb close to them to take photos.
